passage:
For forty-one years, Ida Brannock walked out to the white box on the schoolhouse lawn in Wendle Cross at nine each morning, read the two instruments inside, a rain gauge and a thermometer, and wrote both figures in a handwritten ledger begun in 1938. In all that time the record shows one gap: eleven blank lines one February, when a fall on the ice kept her in hospital. Her rule was that no other person's figures went into the ledger, so the lines stayed empty.

This spring, at seventy-eight, she stepped down as keeper, and the idea of a sensor came from the parish council. Its letter to the district weather office at Lowmarch, asking for a sensor so that nobody need cross the frozen lawn at nine again, brought one for a month's trial, and in March the council voted to buy it. Ida, asked her wish, said only that the white box should stay where it stood.

Neve Callan, who teaches the older class at the village school, had offered her pupils to take the nine o'clock reading in turns, and the office said it would take figures from a machine or a child alike, as long as they passed its checks. The council's chair thanked her, but the council kept to its choice. In April the sensor went up beside the box, which stayed.

In the first hard frost its battery failed, and the office's tables now show eleven blank days for Wendle Cross, the same count as Ida's one February. The office has since asked that someone check the sensor daily, and so at nine each morning, whichever pupil has the turn makes a charge across the frozen lawn.

The pupil wipes the frost from the sensor, checks its small green light, and writes in a notebook that the machine is working. The notebook is ruled in columns, like Ida's ledger, and it has gained a line every morning since. The council's notice about the sensor is still pinned in the school porch. It promises the village an end to the walk across the lawn.

For many summers Tamsin Rowe has led a July walk through the Hatherby cutting, where a railway once ran between an old platform and a brick footbridge. Rowe's first walk found 16, and the usual total is now about ninety. Last July the count fell to 28.

The walk follows the same pattern each year. On a still night, volunteers with red torches set out from the platform and take about 23 minutes to reach the footbridge, marking each green light on a map. Since the trust began locking the platform gate at ten, they have started an hour earlier, at half past nine.

Every light is a wingless female glow-worm. What she needs is a tall grass stem to climb after full dark, where she glows to draw flying males; her larvae live in the turf and feed on snails. That spring the cutting had changed: the Hatherby Line Trust put up 35 solar lamps at the platform end, widened the path with gravel, and had its contractor do the mowing of the banks in May rather than September. The trust's first step after the low count was to switch the lamps off for the rest of the summer.

In August the trust held a meeting in the village hall, and Rowe brought her maps. Her own walk at the old hour of half past ten had found much the same low total. The losses were spread evenly: under the lamps and past them, on the mown banks and on the steep strip below the footbridge beyond reach of the mowing, along the new gravel and on the far bank well away from it. One record followed them. After a dry spring, her 42 snail boards had come up nearly bare, and where snails were scarcest the lights were scarcest too.

Rowe had bought the boards herself after the trust's committee voted against paying for them. The committee has since told its members that the weather was to blame and that switching the lamps off was a sensible precaution. The boards, and the six weeks of mornings the volunteers spent lifting them, get no mention.

passage:
The radio warned of frost at supper: minus four by dawn, with the apricots in full blossom. Tomas went out first to read the thermometer nailed to the gate. From there he looked over the blossoms on the corner tree, the old tree his father had planted by the gate, walked down to the young trees in the far row, and went on to the barn to count the cans of oil: eleven, enough for the burners under half the orchard. Last of all he looked across the lane at Mrs. Odell's orchard.

After supper he drew a plan of the rows on the back of an envelope: a ring of burners round the corner tree, which gave the best fruit on the place, and a double line down the far row, where he thought the cold would settle. The plan needed fifteen cans. The other four, he said, would come across the lane.

They came at nine, in Mrs. Odell's wheelbarrow. Her own trees stood up on the ridge, above the cold, and she had judged that her oil would do more good shared. She had come to help, and she stayed. Between her cans and his, the burners reached every tree on the place, and after midnight it was she who kept them lit until dawn.

Near two, Mrs. Odell judged that the worst of the cold was over and wanted to let the far row burn down. Tomas kept it going, guarding the hollow with care, and at four, when the frost lay white and the thermometer touched minus five, the far row would have been lost without it.

By morning every tree had come through: the whole orchard saved. The cans were empty. Then the radio put the next frost on Friday, and the oil truck could not come until Monday. I was to take the train home on Thursday, and Mrs. Odell would be at her sister's. Tomas, who had coughed through most of the night, stacked the empty cans and said he would manage on his own. That evening I saw him at the gate again, reading the thermometer.
